title: Infra: GPU Fleet, Capacity & IaC + CI/CD Runbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates operational guidance and engineering standards for managing Redwood's GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for procurement, provisioning, and runbook-driven incident response.

Goals
- Maintain a cost-effective GPU fleet with predictable throughput for inference workloads.
- Standardize Terraform modules, naming, and CI/CD patterns to reduce drift and accelerate safe changes.
- Define clear runbooks for alerts, capacity emergencies, upgrades, and rollbacks.

Scope
- GPU instance pools (hosted Dedicated and Private customers), autoscaling policies, and warm pools.
- Cloud accounts (AWS primary), VPC networking, private link / peering, subnets, and IAM guardrails.
- Terraform modules used for GPU node groups, autoscaling, networking, and monitoring.
- CI/CD pipelines that publish IaC changes, AMI/container builds, and runtime config.

1) GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning\n
Summary:
- We operate mixed-generation NVIDIA GPU pools (A100 40GB, A100 80GB, H100, and T4 for light workloads). Pools are divided by SKU and purpose: inference-low-latency, inference-batch, training-ephemeral.

Key metrics to monitor (SLOs and thresholds):
- Node Availability SLO: 99.9% per region per month.
- P99 Request Latency: <= 250ms for low-latency routes (measured at ingress).
- CPU/GPU Utilization target: steady-state 55–75% for dedicated pools; spikes up to 90% allowed for <= 2 hours.
- Queue Length / Backlog Threshold: if queued requests > 50 for > 5m, trigger capacity-scaling and paging.

Capacity Sizing Guidelines:
- Baseline sizing: estimate tokens/sec per GPU for representative model, then compute needed GPUs = ceil(requests_per_sec * avg_tokens / tokens_per_sec_per_gpu).
- Buffer policy: maintain 15% spare headroom for autoscale cooldowns + scheduled maintenance.
- Warm pool: maintain 10% of fleet (min 2 nodes) pre-warmed (AMI booted, health checks passing) to avoid cold-start latency.

Autoscaling & Policies:
- Use horizontal node scaling by node pool. Scaling triggers: (1) sustained GPU utilization > 70% for 3m; (2) queue length > 30 for 2m.
- Scaling cooldown: 5m for scale-up, 10m for scale-down.
- Maximum burst: configured per pool (default: 2x baseline up to account quota).

Maintenance Windows & Draining:
- Weekly maintenance window: Sundays 02:00–05:00 UTC (non-peak).
- Draining: nodes are cordoned + requests gradually shifted with KV cache continuation. Drain policy: stop scheduling new requests, wait up to 300s for existing inflight tokens, then force-terminate if necessary.

2) Cloud Accounts & Networking Standards

Account Structure:
- AWS org with accounts: prod-core, prod-dedicated, staging, sandbox, infra-tools. No customer workloads in sandbox accounts.
- Cross-account roles follow naming: redwood-<env>-infra-admin, redwood-<env>-read-only.

VPC & Subnet Design:
- VPC per region + account. Standard CIDR blocks: 10.<env>.<region>.0/16 (examples documented in account registry).
- Subnets: private-app, private-gpu, public-loadbalancer. GPU pools must live in private-gpu subnets with route to NAT gateway.
- NACLs and Security Groups: deny-all-by-default, allow only necessary ports. GPU nodes: allow egress to S3, ECR, STS, internal controlplane ports (TCP 2200, 50051, 8080).

Networking Patterns for Private Deployments:
- Support VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway for customer connections. Where possible prefer PrivateLink for control-plane endpoints.
- Egress IP consistency: use NAT gateways with Elastic IP pools for enterprise customers that require allowlisting.

DNS and Service Discovery:
- Use Route53 private hosted zones per account; service names follow: <service>.<env>.<region>.svc.redwood.internal

3) Terraform / IaC Modules (Standards & Catalog)

Module ownership and versioning:
- All modules live in the infra-git monorepo under /modules. Modules must include: README, examples/, CHANGELOG.md, and semantic version tags.
- Release process: bump major/minor/patch via PR, approvals required from module owners and infra-arch. CI builds module artifacts and publishes a version tag.

Canonical modules (short catalog table):
| module | purpose | required inputs | outputs | owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpu-node-pool | Provision GPU node groups (ASG/GKE nodepools) | sku, desired_capacity, min,max, instance_profile | node_pool_id, autoscale_policy | infra-gpu |
| vpc-core | Create VPC, subnets, route tables | cidr, region, env | vpc_id, subnet_ids | infra-network |
| iam-fine-grained | Standard IAM roles/policies | service, env, principals | role_arn | infra-iam |
| monitoring-agent | CloudWatch/Datadog agent installs | env, tags | dm_endpoint | infra-monitoring |

Terraform best-practices (rules):
- Use remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking. State paths: s3://redwood-iac-state/<account>/<region>/<stack>.tfstate
- Keep short, composable modules < 300 LOC. Avoid provider overrides inside modules.
- Enforce pre-commit and tflint, terraform validate in CI.
- PR requirements: 2 approvers for infra modules, 1 approver for stack-level changes.

Example snippet (gpu-node-pool usage):
```hcl
module "gpu_inference_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-git.git//modules/gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.12.0"
  sku = "a100-80gb"
  desired_capacity = 12
  min = 4
  max = 24
  instance_profile = "redwood-gpu-instance-profile"
  tags = { team = "infra-gpu", env = "prod" }
}
```

4) CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Pipeline types:
- IaC pipeline (terraform): lint -> plan -> manual gate -> apply. Runs in infra CI account with ephemeral credentials.
- AMI/container build pipeline: packer/buildkite -> image tests -> publish to AMI/ECR -> promote.
- Runtime config deploys: config repo -> staged rollout -> canary -> global.

CI rules and gates:
- Terraform plan artifacts must be uploaded and linked in PR. Applies to prod require a manual approval from oncall + infra owner.
- Golden AMI promotion requires blue-green test suite pass and approval by infra-release.
- Security scan (Trivy / tfsec) must pass with no high/critical findings; otherwise block merge.

Example CI stages (high-level):
1) Pre-commit checks (tflint, pre-commit hooks).
2) Pull request: terraform fmt, validate, plan. Plan comment posted on PR.
3) Infra QA: integration tests in staging (smoke up to 4 nodes).
4) Manual approval for prod apply.
5) Apply executed via pipeline role; outputs stored in S3.

Artifact promotion and rollbacks:
- AMI/ECR tags: use semantic tags + build-id (e.g., inference-a100:v1.4.3+build-20260209).
- Rollback: redeploy previous artifact tag via automated pipeline. Documented rollback playbook below.

5) Runbooks & Incident Response (GPU-related incidents)

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- High GPU saturation: metric gpu_utilization.p95 > 90% for 3m -> P1 alert.
- Node termination rate: > 3 nodes terminated in 5m -> P1.
- High error rate: 5xx rate > 2% for 5m on inference route -> P1/P2 depending on customer impact.

On-call steps (P1):
1) Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty within 5m.
2) Check dashboards: cluster capacity, node pool health, queue length, autoscaler events.
3) If autoscaler failed to scale: check scaling policies, AWS ASG events, resource quotas. Attempt manual scale up via terraform workspace override or AWS console.
4) If nodes are unhealthy: collect journalctl, docker/container runtime logs, describe instance status, and check kernel OOM or GPU driver errors.
5) If cross-region failover required: promote secondary pool via routing policy and update loadbalancer weights.
6) Post-incident: create postmortem within 72h with RCA and action items.

Escalation matrix:
- 0–15m: oncall infra engineer.
- 15–60m: infra senior engineer.
- >60m: infra lead and SRE manager; paging to product ops if customer-impacting.

Common runbook actions (with commands):
- Manual scale up (AWS example):
  aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name redwood-prod-gpu-a100 --desired-capacity 16 --honor-cooldown

- Drain node (Kubernetes example):
  kubectl cordon <node>
  kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=300

- Rebuild image (short):
  ./ci/build-image.sh --sku a100-80gb --version v1.4.3

6) Upgrade & Rollback Playbook

Planned upgrade (kernel, driver, AMI):
1) Create upgrade RFC and schedule in maintenance calendar.
2) Bake image and deploy to staging with smoke tests.
3) Canary 5% of traffic for 30m; monitor latency, error rate, GPU loading.
4) If metrics stable, ramp to 25% then to 100% (rolling by AZ).
5) If regression found, immediately pause rollout and execute rollback.

Rollback steps (fast path):
- Revert to previous AMI/ECR tag via deployment pipeline.
- If rollback fails, shift routing away from impacted pool and open cross-team incident.

7) Ownership, SLAs & Runbook Maintenance

Owners
- infra-gpu: primary owner for node pools, autoscaling policies, and AMI pipelines.
- infra-network: VPC, routing, connectivity, and account boundaries.
- infra-ci: pipelines, pre-commit hooks, and release automation.

Documentation hygiene
- Runbooks must be reviewed quarterly. Any change to autoscaling logic or critical thresholds requires a short change record and one-week staged rollout.
- Post-incident playbook updates are mandatory for any P1/P2 with >30m customer impact.

Appendix: Quick checklist for triage
- Are autoscalers failing? Check cloud provider quotas and ASG events.
- Is there an AMI rollback needed? Verify last successful AMI test and tag.
- Are network rules blocking control plane? Validate SGs, NACLs, and route tables.
- Do we have sufficient spare capacity? Check warm pool and account quotas.

Contact list
